morning.title: Supreme Court acquits school officials in Maharashtra tribal girl’s death in 2020 pillar collapse
morning.text:
Supreme Court acquits school officials in Maharashtra tribal girl’s death in 2020 pillar collapse
The Bench said the school administrators could not be held criminally responsible merely for failing to ensure the pillar was properly constructed.
The Supreme Court has acquitted the president and hostel superintendent of a Maharashtra tribal residential school of culpable homicide charges over the death of a 12-year-old girl who was crushed when a poorly constructed pillar collapsed on her in 2020.
In a judgment released on Thursday, the court held that a mere breach of duty or failure to ensure proper construction was insufficient to establish criminal liability in the absence of requisite knowledge or proof of gross negligence.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan said the school administrators could not be held criminally responsible merely for failing to ensure proper construction of the pillar, particularly when the actual construction work had been entrusted to a contractor.
“The mere failure to attain the standard of care prescribed by the law, thereby committing breach of such duty as observed by the high court would not be a criminal act,” noted the bench, setting aside the Bombay High Court’s February 2026 order refusing to quash the criminal proceedings against the two school officials.
The court emphasised that culpable homicide under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof of intention or knowledge that the act was likely to cause death, and that the mere use of inferior construction material could not, by itself, establish that the school administrators knew that the construction was likely to cause a student’s death.
The case
The case arose from the February 15, 2020 incident at Prashnachinha Adivasi Ashram Shala in Mangrul Chawala in Maharashtra's Amravati district, where Bharti Belsare, a Class 7 student, died after a cement-and-brick pillar collapsed on her. Several other girls were also injured in the incident.
Her father, a labourer, lodged an FIR alleging that the school’s president, Matin Shankarrao Bhosale and the hostel superintendent had deliberately permitted substandard construction and failed to take adequate precautions, resulting in the pillar collapsing on the children. Following an investigation, police filed a chargesheet against the two under Section 304 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) read with Section 34 (joint criminal liability) of the IPC.
The high court had declined to quash the proceedings, holding that forensic examination of the construction material revealed inadequate cement content and that the pillar lacked a proper solid base. It concluded that there was sufficient material to indicate a breach of duty by the school officials and that they had knowledge that substandard construction could cause harm or death.
What the Supreme Court said
The Supreme Court, however, drew a distinction between culpable homicide under Section 304 and causing death by negligence under Section 304A of the IPC, pointing out that the latter provision covers cases where death is caused by a rash or negligent act without intention or knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.
Explaining the distinction, the bench said Section 304A applies only where there is neither intention to cause death nor knowledge that the act would, in all probability, result in death. Where intention or knowledge is the motivating force behind the act, the more serious charge of culpable homicide would apply.
The court also made it clear that even a charge under Section 304A requires more than ordinary negligence.
“Mere negligence cannot be construed to mean rashness,” said the bench, adding that criminal negligence must involve “gross and culpable neglect” or a failure to take precautions that it was imperative for the accused to adopt.
It said the prosecution must establish that the accused’s act was the direct and proximate cause of death, and not merely one of several circumstances that contributed to the incident. Referring to the legal principle of “causa causans” -- the immediate and effective cause, the bench said criminal liability under Section 304A cannot be fastened merely because an act was a necessary condition for the eventual death.
Applying this test, the court held that the school administrators’ alleged failure to ensure proper construction could not be regarded as the immediate and effective cause of Bharti’s death.
“Many other factors might have resulted in the unfortunate incident,” said the bench, pointing out that the contractor and his team were actually undertaking the construction. Had the contractor taken adequate care to ensure the safety of the students, the incident might not have occurred, it added.
The bench further said the school officials stood on a different footing from other accused, if any, in the case, and that the person who could prima facie be held responsible for the girl’s death was the contractor, subject to evidence that may emerge during the trial.
Towards the end of the judgment, the court acknowledged the tragedy and the anguish of the victim’s parents but cautioned against allowing the outcome of an incident to influence the application of criminal law.
“Dictating this order was a very painful experience. The very thought of a twelve-year-old girl getting crushed beneath the pillar of her own school makes our heart bleed with pain and agony,” it said.

Traffic curbs in place between Nov 5-15 around Anand Vihar ISBT amid festival rush
morning.text:
The Delhi Traffic Police has put in place special traffic arrangements on roads around Anand Vihar inter-state bus terminal (ISBT) and adjoining transport hubs from November 5 to 15 to manage the anticipated surge in passenger movement during the festive season, two senior police officers said.
Additionally, the traffic police have also issued an advisory, warning the public about the possible traffic commotion likely to be caused by heavy movement of passengers and informing them about the restrictions and diversions implemented on the roads.
According to the advisory, two arterial roads – Chaudhary Charan Singh Marg (also known as Road No-56), connecting Dilshad Garden with Ghazipur roundabout, and Swami Dayanand Marg (Road No-57), connecting the Ghazipur flyover with Shahdara flyover via Jagatpuri and Hasanpur Depot – are likely to remain affected due to the festive rush at the transport hubs around the Anand Vihar.
Anand Vihar is a major transport hub for migrants from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand, as a majority of trains towards such states originate and culminate from the Anand Vihar Terminal railway station. Uttar Pradesh-bound government buses operate from Anand Vihar interstate bus terminal as well as from the UP government’s bus terminal at Kaushambi, which are separated by Chaudhary Charan Singh Marg. Also, hundreds of buses operated by private players also move towards such states from areas around the Ghazipur border.
“During the festive season. tens of thousands of people reach Anand Vihar daily to leave for their hometowns in trains and buses. As a result, the areas around the transport hub are flooded with passengers, which leads to massive traffic jams on the connecting roads,” said a senior police officer, aware of the traffic arrangement plans.
Traffic diversions and parking restrictions
Through the advisory, the traffic police said that the Ghazipur roundabout and the Ramprastha-Vivek Vihar road have been turned as the traffic restriction and diversion points. Commuters travelling towards NH-24, Sarai Kale Khan and Barapullah corridor have been advised to avoid Chaudhary Charan Singh and Swami Dayanand Margs and instead use the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway via Grand Trunk (GT) Road.
Similarly, those travelling towards Ghaziabad and Dilshad Garden from central, and south Delhi areas have been asked to use the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway near Akshardham and reach their destinations via GT Road.
“Parking, waiting or halting all vehicles, including buses, auto-rickshaws and taxis, will be strictly prohibited on either carriageway of Chaudhary Charan Singh Marg (Road No-56), particularly near Anand Vihar ISBT entry/exit points. Motorists are advised to use the designated parking spaces on Kaushambi Road near Maruti showroom and Kaushambi Road DDA land near NH-24, subject to availability and approved arrangements,” the advisory said.

morning.title: From rank-based admissions to lower fees: Decoding NMC's proposed NEET-PG reforms
morning.text:
From rank-based admissions to lower fees: Decoding NMC's proposed NEET-PG reforms
The proposed changes also include greater digitisation of counselling, lower fees for non-clinical courses, and a review of residents’ stipends, among others.
Postgraduate medical admissions in India could undergo a significant overhaul starting with the 2027 counselling cycle, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) proposing to replace the existing percentile-based qualifying system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS with a rank-only system.
The proposed changes also include greater digitisation of counselling, lower fees for non-clinical courses, a review of residents’ stipends and biometric verification to prevent candidates from blocking seats.
The proposals are part of the recommendations of a 12-member expert committee constituted by the Union health ministry on July 23, following the Supreme Court’s intervention in a case challenging the sharp reduction in NEET-PG qualifying cut-offs. The Centre has submitted the committee’s report containing findings and recommendations to the court in an affidavit on Tuesday.
The reforms aim to address two recurring concerns: vacant postgraduate medical seats and delays in counselling that affect the start of the academic session. However, the rank-only proposal is yet to be incorporated into final regulations and formally notified.
Here is what could change and how it would differ from the current system.
No more percentile-based qualifying cut-offs?
Under the existing system, candidates must secure a prescribed minimum percentile to become eligible for postgraduate medical counselling. A percentile indicates a candidate’s relative performance compared with other test-takers. The authorities can lower the qualifying percentile when seats remain vacant, thereby expanding the pool of candidates eligible for admission.
This was at the centre of the controversy following the NEET-PG 2025 counselling process. On January 13, 2026, the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) reduced the qualifying percentile for reserved-category candidates to zero, making candidates scoring as low as minus 40 out of 800 eligible for admission. For general and Economically Weaker Section candidates, the cut-off was reduced from the 50th percentile to the seventh percentile.
The decision followed around 9,000 postgraduate seats remaining vacant after the second round of counselling. It was challenged in the Supreme Court by social worker Harisharan Devgan and doctors, who argued that allowing candidates with zero or negative scores to qualify could dilute minimum standards in medical education.
What is proposed: Instead of declaring qualifying percentiles and lowering them to make more candidates eligible, candidates would be ranked according to their performance, with counselling conducted based on these ranks.
The affidavit states: “NMC is in the process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised, wherein only a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS counselling will be adopted; no percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates.”
NMC secretary Dr Raghav Langer communicated the decision to the Director General of Health Services (DGHS) on October 1, according to the affidavit. A senior NMC official told HT that the proposal had been approved in principle, but “the commission would wait for the court’s final directions before proceeding with the next steps, including seeking stakeholders’ suggestions.”
The panel has also cautioned that the change should not compromise minimum standards. “The sanctity of NEET examinations should be maintained, and minimum qualifying standards in postgraduate medical education are not diluted to the extent of permitting candidates with grossly inadequate or negative performance to become eligible for admission,” the affidavit said.
Counselling to become more digital
The committee found that counselling delays were partly linked to manual processes and to gaps in coordination among the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC), the NMC, colleges, and state authorities.
Two preliminary MCC audit meetings, held on May 20 and June 3, flagged the reliance on colleges for manual verification of seat matrices, delays in adding newly approved seats and repeated extensions of counselling timelines.
Until 2025, MCC depended on colleges to provide and verify seat details. The process was complicated by the fact that newly approved seats could be added by NMC after the first round had begun, requiring further verification and changes to the counselling schedule.
Candidates also had to physically visit colleges to complete admission formalities, submit original documents and seek their return when upgrading to another seat. The committee flagged delays and inconvenience linked to document release and fee refunds.
What is proposed: The panel has recommended that NMC share an updated and verified seat matrix with MCC well before counselling begins. It has also proposed online sharing of NEET-UG, NEET-PG, MDS and super-speciality examination results with state counselling authorities.
A feasibility study for sharing results online with state authorities is under way for the 2027 academic year. The committee has called for counselling to be digitised with minimal human intervention and for MCC to develop standard operating procedures and a project charter that define the responsibilities of different stakeholders.
The charter would also record changes ordered by courts or competent authorities as “institutional memory”, the report said. MCC has been asked to prepare summary reports after each counselling exercise and hold stakeholder meetings before and after counselling.
What has already changed: Some processes have been introduced in the 2026-27 counselling cycle. These include online release of candidates who upgrade their seats, allowing candidates to accept upgraded seats without first physically returning to their earlier colleges, and changes to fee- and document-related procedures. The report also records the introduction of a query-resolution mechanism, informational videos and an online dashboard.
Lower fees for non-clinical courses
The committee has flagged vacancies in pre-clinical and para-clinical postgraduate disciplines, which generally attract fewer candidates than clinical specialities such as general medicine, surgery and paediatrics.
It has recommended that state fee fixation committees consider charging lower fees for non-clinical courses to encourage candidates to take up these seats.
“The fee of non-clinical branches may be a little less so that the candidates feel encouraged to accept the seat and this wastage of medical seats may be prevented,” the report said.
The panel has also suggested considering exemptions from compulsory service bonds for candidates admitted to pre-clinical and para-clinical subjects, leaving the decision to state governments.
Stipends, rural incentives and seat-blocking checks
The committee has called for addressing disparities in stipends between clinical and non-clinical branches, and recommended that states consider incentives for doctors willing to serve in rural areas. It has also suggested reviewing the duration and monetary provisions of compulsory service bonds in consultation with stakeholders.
For BDS and BSc Nursing courses, the panel has flagged vacancies and recommended improving employment opportunities for graduates. It has been suggested to consider discontinuing seats that remain vacant for two to three consecutive years and rationalising fees.
To prevent candidates from appearing in examinations multiple times to block seats, the committee has asked NBEMS and the National Testing Agency (NTA) to explore the use of KYC and biometric verification during entrance examinations.
Why are the changes being considered?
265,980 candidates took NEET-PG 2026 for 63,177 postgraduate medical seats. The previous counselling cycle saw thousands of seats remain vacant, prompting authorities to lower qualifying cut-offs to widen the pool of eligible candidates.
The Supreme Court, while hearing the challenge to the January 2026 cut-off reduction, asked the Centre to explain how the decision would preserve standards in medical education. On May 4, it directed the creation of an institutional mechanism to examine recurring issues in the NEET-PG admission process. The health ministry subsequently formed the expert committee, headed by DGHS director general Dr Loveneesh G Krishna, with representatives from NMC, NBEMS, MCC and other bodies.
Doctors have questioned whether moving away from percentile-based results would, by itself, address concerns over the dilution of qualifying standards.
“Qualifying percentile is not a mere administrative formality; it is the minimum benchmark intended to safeguard academic standards and ultimately the quality of specialists in healthcare. It will be a huge injustice with merit if minimum admission criteria are diluted drastically,” said Dr Raj Shekhar Yadav, one of the petitioners in the case.
“Changing the examination formula does not erase the questions surrounding the drastic reduction of qualifying cut-offs. Vacant seats cannot become an excuse to compromise merit, dilute qualifying standards or experiment with the future of medical education,” said Dr Dhruv Chauhan, chairperson of the Legal Cell for All India Doctors.
A DGHS official, however, defended the proposed changes, saying they were intended to benefit candidates and shorten the counselling process.
“We have made these reforms in the interest of the candidates... The new reforms will also reduce the counselling time, which will subsequently help candidates to start their academic session on time,” the official said.
The proposals are targeted at the 2027 counselling cycle, but their implementation will depend on the finalisation of NMC regulations, the Supreme Court’s directions and consultations with stakeholders.

morning.title: In age of flux, India must not shy away from risks, bold reforms
morning.text:
In age of flux, India must not shy away from risks, bold reforms
The geopolitical flux is undoubtedly challenging, but countries with an ability to take risks and carry out bold reforms can find crucial opportunities even in this scenario. India must not fight shy of doing it.
At the recently concluded Kautilya Economic Conclave, external affairs minister S Jaishankar spoke about an “age of flux” but exuded confidence that the government managed to hold India in a sweet spot, which he conceded was not static but kept shifting. That said, India faces profound challenges, both internal and external, because of the geopolitical flux that is a harsh reality. Before we address India’s challenges, it would be useful to understand the main features and implications of the geopolitical flux that the world is currently witnessing.
The most important actor driving this, without a shadow of doubt, is the US, which under President Donald Trump, has embarked on a reordering of the international relations system as we know it after World War II. Three things about this are noteworthy. One, the US has concluded that the existing order strategically disadvantages it, carries an unacceptable price, and allows other major countries a free ride. Two, the changes underway in America’s foreign and security policy will likely outlast President Trump. Three, no major power can claim that it has been left untouched by US policy changes. The main strategic implication of this is that US foreign policy retrenchment has become both transactional and unpredictable.
The second feature of the geopolitical flux, unsurprisingly, is China. China presents a conundrum. On the one hand, China is unquestionably America’s peer and while it is running behind on some metrics, it is catching up fast. On the other hand, China really runs the risk of getting old before it becomes rich. In addition, President Xi Jinping confronts political headwinds at home although given the level of opacity in China, the extent of discontent is in doubt. Xi Jinping has continued for way too long as President and can justify his long reign only with something dramatic like the reunification of Taiwan or demonstrable subordination of America by China in some way. The main strategic implication of this is that Beijing may become more assertive and conflictual.
The third feature is the demise of multilateralism and other countries being left to their own devices. The dysfunctional UN Security Council, the irrelevance of the World Trade Organization and the near-total collapse of the alliance system (with NATO leading the way) has left countries, both big and small, scrambling for a response. Canada’s Mark Carney has spoken of a coalition of the “Middle Powers”, but it is becoming obvious that this is easier said than done. The main strategic implication of this is that while the old order has clearly perished, a new one is yet to take its place. This interregnum may neither be transient nor necessarily peaceful.
The fourth feature of the geopolitical flux is that conflicts and crises are rapidly becoming irresolvable, and the cascading effect of this turbulence is to impose great hardships on ordinary people everywhere. The conflict in Ukraine is more than four years old. The war in Iran is already eight months old. Neither shows any sign of abating. The main strategic implication of this is to cause enormous strain on the global order which is already straining at the leash.
The last feature of the geopolitical flux is that it is hard to think of any rules being followed by anyone, when talking of the global order at present. It has become a cliché to say that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. It is easy to say the weak states must hang together, or else they will hang separately.
Nevertheless, we should not discount the ability of the small and weak States to hedge their bets and negotiate their way out of trouble. The main strategic implication of this is that in the absence of clear rules, countries will all practice their own version of ad hoc multi-alignment with a view to advancing their national interests.
So, against the above backdrop, what can India do to navigate this geopolitical flux and safeguard its interests? One obvious answer is to double down on our foreign and security policy of multi-alignment designed to preserve India’s strategic autonomy. But it is worth bearing in mind that multi-alignment is not a static concept but a dynamic one. The scope and depth of engagement that India chooses to have with another, changes over time. These changes can be wrought either by the country practising multi-alignment, namely India or by the country which is the object of it. Similarly, the amount of policy space that India seeks through strategic autonomy is not static and can change over time. On both these things, it can be argued that India has more policy flexibility than is commonly believed. On multi-alignment, it is clear that the US is recalibrating its ties with India (as it is doing with every other country in the world), so India is probably doing the same vis-à-vis the US. This is no bad thing since this can simultaneously give India more strategic space to deal with the EU or even Russia. It has also resulted in careful reassessment of our ties with China. With strategic autonomy meant to preserve policy space, perhaps India can afford to use the policy space acquired in the past for carrying out key domestic economic reforms and for making adjustments to its foreign security and trade policy, both of which are vital to increase its comprehensive national power.
The geopolitical flux is undoubtedly challenging, but countries with an ability to take risks and carry out bold reforms can find crucial opportunities even in this scenario. India must not fight shy of doing it.

morning.title: SC: Not inclined to transfer Tirupati ghee trial out of AP
morning.text:
SC: Not inclined to transfer Tirupati ghee trial out of AP
The Supreme Court on Thursday refused to transfer the trial in the Tirupati “laddu” adulteration case outside Andhra Pradesh observing that the courts are immune from political statements made in the case.
The court passed the order while hearing a transfer petition filed by one of the accused Machindra Shantaram, a Maharashtra-based dairy industry businessman and the Managing Director of Malganga Milk and Agro Products Pvt Ltd. Shantaram, who was represented by senior advocate Siddharth Dave, alleged that continuous statements made by the chief minister and the deputy chief minister have created a “politically surcharged atmosphere”.
“The trial is taking place in a politically surcharged atmosphere, it will prejudice my trial. Nobody can be immune from such statements made by the chief minister and deputy chief minister in the state. I am the only person who will suffer,” Dave said, adding that even though the forensic report had ruled out the presence of animal fat in the ghee, political leaders continued to make such statements.
Citing a “language barrier”, he said: “Please transfer the case to the adjoining state, for free and fair trial. Most of the accused are from North India. There is also a language barrier.”
Refusing the prayer to transfer the trial to a neighbouring state, the bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi said, “Let the trial proceed. Courts are immune from such statements which are made.”
The court added, “Witnesses are from the local area. Allowing your prayer will frustrate the trial,” as it dismissed the petition by stating, “No case for shifting of the trial is made out at this stage.”
The bench further told Dave that it had already taken care of the impartiality of the probe by constituting a Special Investigation Team (SIT) comprising officers of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Andhra Pradesh Police in October 2024.
The CJI said, “Let them continue to make statements. This is why we constituted the SIT. We have already silenced everyone.”

morning.text:
3 contractors arrested after Chawri Bazar building collapse kills two
Chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered the immediate suspension of the junior engineer and assistant engineer concerned.
Delhi Police has arrested three contractors in connection with the collapse of an under-construction building in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar that killed two people and injured two others on Thursday, officials aware of the matter said on Friday.
Police said the three men, who have been booked under Section 105 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), were arrested from Sirohi village in Faridabad’s Dauj tehsil.
Deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh identified the accused as Siraj, Tajuddin and Furkan, all residents of the Ajmeri Gate area. Their full names were not immediately available.
Deep Dive
The arrests come amid questions over how construction continued at the site despite the building allegedly having no sanctioned plan and Delhi Police having alerted the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) about construction activity in the area nearly five months before the collapse.
The building, a ground-plus-three-floor structure in Gali Sitara near Chawri Bazar Metro station, collapsed in two stages around 9.30am on Thursday. The lintel of the third floor reportedly gave way while concrete work was underway, followed by the collapse of the remaining floors within 15 to 20 minutes. Two workers, Kishori, 40, and Sanjeet, 45, died, while two others sustained injuries.
Also Read: Chawri Bazar building collapse: What probes into previous Delhi tragedies found
The collapse also exposed serious enforcement lapses. In a letter dated June 15, the station house officer of Hauz Qazi police station had alerted the deputy commissioner of MCD’s City SP Zone about new residential construction spread over around 70 square yards at property number 4547-48 in Wali Sheesh Mahal, Ajmeri Gate, and sought action.
MCD acknowledged receiving the communication but said its subsequent inspection found the owner undertaking repair work that its maintenance department had advised in April. In its inquiry, the civic body alleged that the owner used the repair advisory as a cover to clandestinely undertake fresh construction on the second and third floors without the requisite permissions.
The MCD inquiry report also flagged the property’s tax declarations, alleging that excess floor coverage had been declared with the mala fide intention of misleading the authorities and claiming protection under laws applicable to older structures.
The rescue operation on Thursday was hampered by the extremely narrow lanes of the walled city, which prevented heavy machinery from reaching the site. Fire personnel and other rescue teams had to rely largely on manual debris removal. Residents of neighbouring buildings were evacuated after police warned that one adjoining structure was in a precarious condition.
Also Read: Chawri Bazar building collapse: Similar incidents that have rocked Delhi
Chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered the immediate suspension of the junior engineer and assistant engineer concerned, a detailed inquiry and an FIR against the contractor. She also directed officials to ensure the best possible treatment for the injured and provide ex-gratia assistance to the victims’ families.
Police are continuing their investigation into the construction activity and the circumstances leading to the collapse.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) has ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls in Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Mizoram, Odisha and Sikkim, even as its contentious Special Intensive Revision (SIR) continues to be under scrutiny
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls in Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Mizoram, Odisha and Sikkim, even as its contentious Special Intensive Revision (SIR) continues to be under scrutiny.
In a letter dated November 4 to the chief electoral officers of the six regions, the poll body fixed January 1, 2027, as the qualifying date. Polling stations are to be rationalised by November 20 and integrated draft rolls published on November 30. Claims and objections can be filed till December 30, and the final rolls will be published on January 21, 2027.
The qualifying date is the cut-off by which a person must have turned 18 to be eligible for enrolment in a given revision. Polling station rationalisation is done before the draft roll so that no station has too many electors, and so that a booth is not placed far from voters, especially those in remote or newly built areas.
The SSR uses existing roll as its starting point, with existing voters’ names generally carried forward to the draft roll. The exercise will be carried out in every state after the SIR is completed. On October 15, ECI had ordered an annual SSR in 17 states and Union Territories.
Under the SSR, officials start with the existing roll, publish a draft and invite claims and objections. Booth-level officers verify new applications, and electoral registration officers (EROs) decide on them before the final roll is published. In the SIR, however, electors are largely asked to fill enumeration forms and the roll is rebuilt from those forms, with voters having to establish their eligibility.
ECI has also built in safeguards against wrongful deletions, the main complaint against the SIR. The number of Form 7 applications, used to object to or seek deletion of a name, that one person can file has been capped at 10 forms per elector during the claims and objections period, and five per month during continuous updation.
The November 4 letteralso mandated the EROs to personally verify cases where deletions exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors, or where the same person is the objector in more than five cases.
For nearly two decades, summary revisions were carried out annually. ECI, however, broke from that when it ordered the SIR on June 24 last year, deviating from the annual SSRs. The exercise was rolled out in phases, with Phase three currently being underway covering 16 states and three Union Territories.
The poll body said SSR schedules for states where SIR is underway or has just ended, including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Delhi and Telangana, will be announced later. For Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, where SIR has not begun, the schedule will be notified keeping weather conditions in mind.
EROs have been told to ensure that no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person is included. They must seek applications from unenrolled adults, those turning 18 by January 1, 2027, and advance applications for those turning 18 on April 1, July 1 and October 1, 2027. The poll body has asked for help desks for migrants and special camps for the homeless and marginalised groups. It has also called for targeted outreach to women, transgender persons, Scheduled Tribes, senior citizens and persons with disabilities.
Political parties will get weekly printed lists of claims and objections, along with free copies of the draft and final rolls. Their booth level agents can submit up to 10 forms a day to booth level officers. If an agent files more than 30 forms during the claims period, the ERO or assistant ERO must verify them.

‘Win-win solution’: Defence secretary hails Agniveer extension, explains why 75% recruits get 2 more years
The extension allows 75 per cent of each batch, who were earlier required to leave after four years, to serve for another two years.
Defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh on Thursday called the revised Agniveer scheme a “win-win solution”, in response to a Cabinet decision allowing recruits a second two-year engagement period.
“You can also call it a Diwali gift,” Singh said, speaking a day after the Cabinet cleared the change on Wednesday. He said the performance of Agniveers, including in various operations, had prompted the decision to offer them a second term.
Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani on Wednesday announced that Union Cabinet approved a two-year extension of service for Agniveers.
Deep Dive
“... 25% of those [Agniveers] who complete their initial four-year engagement period will be enrolled as regular soldiers. Regarding the remaining 75%, the Indian Defence Forces have recommended—and the Cabinet has approved today—that they be granted a second engagement period of two years,” the CDS said.
Under Agnipath recruitment model, soldiers are recruited for a four-year term, with a provision to retain only 25 per cent of them in regular service for another 15 years. The extension allows 75 per cent of each batch, who were earlier required to leave after four years, to serve for another two years.
Also Read: Armed forces need a balance of youth, experience: Chief of Defence Staff
‘Four-year review built into design’
Singh added that the scheme's four-year review mechanism was designed to assess the performance of Agniveers at the end of their initial period and said that the review found their performance strong enough to justify a second term.
The move comes weeks before the three services were to start releasing 75 per cent of Agniveers from their first batch in phases starting mid-November, mounting to over 18,300 personnel.
The 18,300 soldiers, who were to be released this year, account for three-fourths of the 24,400 recruits inducted into the army, air force and navy in the first round of recruitment. The first batch comprised around 19,000 Agniveers in the army, 2,850 in the IAF and 2,550 in the navy, according to official data.
Centre welcomes revised arrangement
Defence minister Rajnath Singh thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the decision, saying it would open a pathway for willing Agniveers to join the regular forces after four or six years of service.
The Opposition, meanwhile, questioned the timing of the extension and argued that it “leaves the human problem untouched”.
Congress leader Pawan Khera called the move an “election gimmick” and questioned what would happen to the 75 per cent after the additional two years, warning that they risk being left “unemployed on the streets”.
Union home minister Amit Shah also hailed the move, saying, “every willing Agniveer will be able to serve for another 2 years”. The BJP welcomed the move, saying it would help keep the Army young and operationally ready.
Retired Rear Admiral Gurinder Singh Jawanda called the move “a very, very welcome change”, saying it brings the arrangement closer to the original induction plan.
Retired Major Mohammed Ali Shah described it as “brilliant”, while Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav said the additional service period would give recruits “more experience, more skills and a stronger financial base”.

The department has deployed 50 QRVs at identified fire hotspots across the city, in addition to 20 motorcycles
Over 150 locations across Delhi, including vulnerable markets and congested neighbourhoods, will be covered by quick response vehicles (QRVs) and motorcycles to ensure firefighters can reach emergency spots faster during Diwali, as the Delhi Fire Service (DFS) steps up its preparedness for the festival.
QRVs and Motorcycles for Faster Response
According to officials aware of the matter, the department has deployed 50 QRVs at identified fire hotspots across the city, in addition to 20 motorcycles, which will help personnel navigate narrow lanes and congested stretches where larger fire tenders may struggle to reach. Areas such as Vijay Chowk, Laxmi Nagar and Acharya Niketan in Mayur Vihar are among the locations where these vehicles will be stationed.
The DFS, a senior official said, has also planned to deploy 15 additional fire tenders near vulnerable markets between 5pm and midnight on November 7-8 to ensure a swift response during the hours when festive activities are likely to be at their peak.

The arrangements cover all 71 fire stations in the city, with officials directed to ensure that vehicles and firefighting equipment remain operational.
“Additional Divisional Officers (ADOs) and Divisional Officers (DOs) have been instructed to inspect fire tenders, conduct surprise visits and check the overall readiness of their respective stations,” the official said.
The department has also kept automobile workshops ready for vehicle repairs and strengthened wireless communication arrangements to ensure smooth coordination during emergencies. All leave for fire personnel has been cancelled in view of the festive deployment.

Control Room and Emergency Calls
“The control room has also been strengthened, with its staffing increased to around 30-35 personnel to ensure that emergency calls are attended to promptly and none go unanswered,” the official said.
Officials said the department had received 269 fire-related calls on Diwali last year. They added that the service had handled a comparable volume of calls during the summer, when the daily count touched around 275 on two occasions in May.

More checks added on EC staff in eye of storm amid row over internal dissent allegations
The November 4 order places IT director general Seema Khanna under Pawan Kumar Sharma and assigns DEC Prakash Rajpurohit a supporting role in election planning.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has ordered a layer of supervision for a top official in charge of IT systems and shared key responsibilities of a senior deputy election commissioner with another officer, against the backdrop of a mounting controversy over allegations of internal dissent in the poll panel.
The November 4 work order comes three months after a controversial July 28 order prompted two election commissioners to write to the cabinet secretary objecting to the changes. To be sure, ECI has told the Supreme Court that the July 28 order was never implemented because of a July 30 order recalling the changes.
ECI places IT director general under senior deputy election commissioner
According to the new order, director general of IT Seema Khanna will be supervised by senior deputy election commissioner Pawan Kumar Sharma. “She would put up files of above mentioned functional divisions through Sr DEC (PKS),” the order said, describing her responsibilities as IT/ICT and grievance/PGRS (public grievance redressal system).
Khanna is at the centre of a controversy over allegations that ECI centralised digital voter roll infrastructure and implemented restrictions in software to stop state officials from accessing voting lists.
Senior deputy election commissioner Maneesh Garg – who issued the controversial July 28 order – retains election planning but will be assisted by deputy election commissioner Prakash Rajpurohit, who also has charge of delimitation. “He will be supported by DEC (PR),” the order said.
As per the new order, besides IT and ICT, Pawan Kumar Sharma handles political parties, election expenditure policy, the observer division and coordination. He also oversees the North East-II, East-II and South-II zones. Khanna will put up files of her divisions through him.
Also read: Supreme Court seeks Centre, ECI reply in plea against CEC legal immunity
Garg retains election planning and EVM responsibilities
Garg retains election planning, EVMs and Election Database Management Division, along with East-I (Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh) and North-III (Uttar Pradesh). Deputy election commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu will look after administration, establishment, electoral rolls and RTI, and Rajpurohit will send election planning files through Garg.
“We can’t call this order a reversal of the July order because the previous order was never implemented,” a senior EC official told HT, adding that the new order was a unanimous decision by the poll panel.
The order assumed significance because it comes roughly three months after election commissioners SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote nearly identical letters to cabinet secretary TV Somanathan in an unprecedented step on July 29. Sandhu’s letter was accompanied by the copy of an order issued by Garg on July 28 allocating work to himself and other EC officials, including Seema Khanna and deputy election commissioner Sanjay Kumar.
Commissioners raised concerns over file routing and lack of consultation
According to a Hindustan Times report dated October 3, the commissioners were concerned about Garg’s decision to change the routing of files of the IT department under Khanna. The files had earlier gone to Sanjay Kumar.
In their confidential letters to the cabinet secretary, the commissioners said Garg was given additional charge of the Administration Division on July 28, while DEC Bhanu Prakash Yeturu was on leave until August 9. Within hours, they said, he issued a work-allocation order covering officers senior and equivalent to him. The letters said the commissioners were not consulted on the decision. Both cited Sections 18(1) and 18(2) of the 2023 CEC/EC Act. Joshi added that a file he asked for from the Administration Division was not provided.
In the Supreme Court, an ECI affidavit said last month that the July 28 order was never implemented after another direction on July 30. The affidavit argued that the correspondence could not be treated as evidence that key special intensive revision decisions were taken without the concurrence of the other commissioners.
The work order and the letters are significant because Khanna and the IT department are at the heart of a controversy after an investigation by the Indian Express said that the new IT protocol/system put in place by Khanna and approved by ECI shut the database of electors (the rolls) from the very people responsible for adding or deleting names, Electoral Registration Officials (EROs).
Also read: ECI gears up to launch major voter enrolment drive in Uttar Pradesh
ECI denies allegations of differences among election commissioners
The Indian Express investigation also reported that there were differences between the election commissioners, and that Joshi and Sandhu had disagreed several times with chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. ECI has denied this and said that all decisions were either unanimous or taken by a majority in keeping with the rules.
But the allegations have sparked sweeping street protests by activists, the Cockroach Janta Party and the parliamentary Opposition, mounting pressure on Gyanesh Kumar. Over the past two months, people have hit the streets, braving Metro closures, internet shutdown, prohibitory orders and 40,000 security personnel who turned the Capital into a virtual fortress and sparked controversy by detaining several agitators. While the Opposition is seeking the removal of Gyanesh Kumar and scrapping the controversial special intensive revision, the BJP blames them for trying to destabilise constitutional bodies to deflect attention from their own political and electoral failures.

morning.title: Threat actor targets Indian fintechs on weekends when defenders aren’t watching
morning.text:
India’s Computer Emergency Response Team has warned the nation’s financial services industry of a “significant escalation” in attacks by what it describes as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor” that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts.

CERT-IN first detected the attacks in October and issued advisory in which it warned digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If the attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money.

On Thursday, the CERT published an update in which it said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents.

“The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response,” the CERT warned.

CERT-IN has decided the attackers need a name and chose “CRAFTY FALCON.”

The security org has also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX pen-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework – all of which have been linked to users who appear to speak Chinese.

CRAFTY FALCON’s tactics see it go looking for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens, or network paths that help it move into production systems.

If it gets in, the crew re-writes victims’ applications so they do things like make unauthorized API calls. Victims’ defenses assume that only legitimate apps would call those APIs, so activity conducted by the re-written apps aren’t flagged as an attack.

Even if victims suspect an attack, they have a lot to cope with because CERT-IN says CRAFTY FALCON creates many “functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.”

The crew also quickly exploits newly discovered vulnerabilities to keep its attacks fresh.

Once it gets a toehold, the criminal crew makes tiny payments of about $0.01 to test if its attacks work. If those transfers work, CRAFTY FALCON makes larger payments. When the target is a cryptocurrency exchange or virtual digital asset service provider, the crew steals wallet keys and empties cryptocurrency wallets.

Vendors of observability tools will be warming up their Indian sales teams today, because CERT-IN’s advice to Indian businesses includes improving their ability to log events, monitor for anomalies in real time, and send alerts. It also urged keeping test environments off the internet, and restricting access to cloud resources because CRAFTY FALCON is fond of using them to run its attacks.

CERT-IN also warns that the attacks are “active and escalating” and therefore worthy of 24x7 monitoring.

Interestingly, the CERT’s advisory mentions attacks on “entities” across banking, financial services, and insurance, but only names the kind of businesses mentioned above as having reported attacks.

The Register points this out because India is home to literally thousands of banks, many of them small operations that sometimes lack basic infosec protections. CRAFTY FALCON therefore has a target-rich environment in India should it choose to expand its activities. ®

morning.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
morning.text:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

morning.title: Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up
morning.text:
If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe.

“We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement.

Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires.

The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets.

But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue.

Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands.

Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks.

The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter.

In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said.

Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures.

How to stay frosty

To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet.

Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities.

“Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise.

Other recommended tactics include:

  • Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks.

  • Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible.

  • Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer.

  • Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list.

  • Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline.

And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

morning.title: AWS Kiro aims to solve identity crisis by adding another identity: bot orchestrator
morning.text:
AWS Kiro, the cloud giant's AI-oriented integrated development environment, isn't the most popular code editor.

That honor goes to Microsoft's Visual Studio Code, at least as measured by Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey.

Kiro might rank 27th among the listed IDEs, but then it's not really an IDE anymore. Having shrugged off reports that it played a role in outages last year, Kiro now styles itself "an agentic development environment" after a brief stint as "an agentic IDE."

It's also the inheritor of Amazon Q Developer coding assistant users, who have been directed to migrate to Kiro.

It's also "an AI-powered development environment that helps you build software from prototype to production." It's "available as a desktop IDE, a command-line interface, a web app, a mobile app, and a personal AI agent (Crew)."

Except that Kiro Crew is also "the persistent, open source development workspace." It's more agent infrastructure – an environment – that supports Kiro Web, IDE, and CLI.

To help get Kiro through its identity crisis and perhaps make it more beloved, AWS is expanding Kiro's remit still further. The cloud giant is launching Kiro Crew bots, recalling similar efforts like OpenAI dots and Grok Bot, as well as Claude Duet and Meta Muse.

Bots in Kiro Crew are software agents that attempt to carry out long-running tasks.

"A bot is a new way to structure and drive agentic work," a Kiro blog post explains.

"Instead of working in isolated sessions, each bot is a named, long-running agent that you define and customize for a specific part of your work. It has its own memory and runs its own sessions so you stop tracking them one by one. Kiro Crew already learns from how you work. Bots change where that learning lives."

There's some appealing anthropomorphism to giving each agent a name and its own tools, permissions, and memories. You're suddenly surrounded by friends.

The possible downside is how that gets billed – there's potential for a lot of duplicated context if your many agents process overlapping data without some form of shared cache.

Given Amazon's concerns about internal token usage and developer complaints about runaway costs in Kiro, it seems other organizations might be curious about the potential expense of keeping bot memory isolated.

In response to our inquiry about the cost of keeping memory separate, an AWS spokesperson said, “All of the Kiro bots bill together through a developer’s existing Kiro plan. Each bot in Kiro Crew has its own memory and sessions, and their learned context is intentionally kept separate so that what one bot learns doesn’t bleed into another’s work. However, all bots operate within the same Kiro Crew workspace, use the same harness, and have access to the same codebase, project files, MCP, skills, and tools—so they don’t need to independently rediscover your project structure.”

In any event, figuring out how Kiro Crew agents are spending tokens looks likely to require analytics of some sort, because AWS Kiro subscriptions are sold as "credits" that get converted to tokens at different rates, depending on the underlying model.

As a thought experiment, AWS suggests a developer might deploy an intake bot for reading trouble or job tickets, labeling them, flagging duplicates, and drafting reproduction steps for bugs.

Then there might be the build-health bot for checking the CI pipeline periodically and surfacing test failures that require the attention made scarce by having to deal with a bunch of AI agents.

A code review bot might also be warranted for reviewing pull requests and other delegated responsibilities. And top that off with a release-readiness bot, for confirming that merged changes have tests and for seeking release sign-off.

For those smitten by the idea of a single surface through which multiple agents can be configured, routed, and governed, Kiro Crew has your backend. ®

morning.title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
morning.text:
Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks.

News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool.

“The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email.

For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year.

The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent.

Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained.

According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said.

Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem.

“Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.”

In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while.

“Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.”

Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them.

Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems.

Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over.

“Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed.

morning.title: Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets
morning.text:
With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.

While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star's light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope's configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.

Point spreads

Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.

morning.title: Keenan-Reuben murder case: The tragedy that changed a village
morning.text:
Keenan-Reuben murder case: The tragedy that changed a village
In the Catholic-dominated gaothan, a memorial pillar ‘dedicated to the memory of Keenan Santos & Reuben Fernandez’ stands tall at a busy junction.
Social worker Ritasha D’souza was eight years old when Amboli, her cosmopolitan neighbourhood in Andheri West, made national headlines over the killing of two men—Keenan Santos, 24, and Reuben Fernandez, 29--for protecting their female friends from sexual harassment on the street. By the time D’souza began her postgraduate studies in social work years later, “neighbourhood heroes” Keenan and Reuben had become part of the academic discourse on violence against women.
“Aren’t you from Amboli?’ People in my class would ask. ‘You must know all about the incident’, they would say,” D’souza told HT, speaking two days before Bombay High Court upheld the conviction of the main accused Jitendra Fakirchand Rana. The court’s order on Thursday sentencing Rana to life imprisonment while acquitting two other men of murder, brings the curtain down on a case that tested a city which prides itself on being the safest city for women in India.
The 2011 attack
On the night of October 20, 2011, a group of seven friends—four men and three women—had gone to the Amboli Kitchen Bar and Restaurant to watch an India-England cricket match on the big screen. The group had just exited the restaurant after the match when four men—not known in the neighbourhood-- began pawing the women in the group and making lewd comments. While Keenan Santos verbally confronted the molesters, his friend Avinash Solanki slapped one of the men, all of whom fled shorty after. Only to return armed with knives, cricket bats and stumps. In the melee that followed, Jitendra Rana and Satish Dulgaj repeatedly stabbed Keenan Santos and Reuben Fernandez while their two accomplices, Sunil Both and Dipak Piwal, attacked Reuben’s brother Benjamin and Avinash Solanki. The grievously injured Keenan died hours after the attack, Reuben died days later in hospital.
The attacks, on the women and then the killings of Keenan Santos and Reuben Fernandez, on a busy road left the city stunned. “More so since it’s rare that men physically stand up to defend their women friends being harassed. It was sad that the outcome of that was so tragic.,” says advocate Audrey Dmello, director of Majlis Legal Centre, Mumbai, “But still, a message went out. This was before the Nirbhaya case (2012) and before the amendments made to the Indian Penal Code (in cases of violence against women).”
A village remembers
A village remembers
In the Catholic-dominated gaothan (literally a village—Mumbai has 52 demarcated gaothans within its city limits) a memorial pillar ‘dedicated to the memory of Keenan Santos & Reuben Fernandez’ stands tall at a busy junction down the road from St Blaise church. The dust that engulfs most parts of a city—under perennial construction-- hasn’t spared the black granite plaque, partly concealing the names of the two men. But in Amboli, for the local parish and the families of the seven friends, the High Court judgment is a closure or sorts. Keenan’s younger brother Sheldon told HT, “He was a warrior. Even when faced with danger, his first instinct was to ensure his girlfriend’s safety. He stood up for his female friends and their dignity.
“They (Keenan and Rueben) are always cited as examples of bravery. What they did was not only about protecting women, it was about protecting your friends, protecting one another,” said D’souza.
Sheldon’s twin Shane who gave up his career in hospitality to pursue law after Keenan’s murder—both were 18 at that time—says the murders shook up the administration. “We had a lot of support. The government too did its part and appointed a good public prosecutor. There was real action when all four accused were convicted and sentenced to life in 2016. And then we got to know that they had filed appeals in the Bombay High Court. My father who fought so hard all these years could not really get closure because he passed away last year before the appeals were decided,” said Shane who now practises in the Bombay High Court.
The High Court verdict
One of the four accused, Satish Dulgaj, died while in prison, and on Thursday, a division bench of Justices Makarand Karnik and Sandesh D Patil held that there was no cogent evidence to convict Sunil Omprakash Both and Deepak Piwal of the charge of murder. Instead, these two men who had attacked Reuben’s brother Benjamin and his friend Avinash Solanki with cricket bats and stumps on that night of October 20,2011, were convicted for causing simple hurt.
Reuben Fernandez’s family moved to Goa after his killing while the three women who had accompanied Keenan and Reuben that night have since left the city. The incident was as devastating for them as it was for the Santos and Fernandez families, said Shane. Even the Amboli Bar and Kitchen where the boys had their last meal shut down within a few months of the tragedy. In its place stands a line of brighly lit shops in stark contrast to the quaint single-storey cottages in the gaothan on the other side of the road.
A septuagenarian parishioner of St. Blaise Church who prefers to be known only as “Mr Pereira”, remembers Keenan, Rueben, their killing, and the loss that their neighbourhood had collectively felt. “In 2011, there was no violence in Amboli. It was a peaceful place. The incident was as shocking as it was unfortunate. And soon after, there was fear in the minds of people. Nobody wanted to step out at night. Over time, people’s memory has faded but often when I cross that spot (where Amboli bar and kitchen was located) I think of those brave boys,” he said.
In Mumbai, the rising graph of crimes against women as per the NCRB data remains worrying. In 2024 the city recorded the second-highest number of crimes against women (6358) from among 19 metropolitan cities. Though it was still a distant second to Delhi which recorded 13,396 cases. “We should not benchmark crime in a city based on NCRB data because it just means Mumbai is reporting more crime,” cautions Majlis’s Audrey Dmello. “Mumbai is comparatively safe but we have to stop making these comparisons with Delhi. It’s the state capital, millions of girls are out working and the city has to provide them a safe environment,” said Dmello.
For Shane Santos, even though it’s hard to articulate the pain the family has undergone since Keenan’s death, he says, he understands that what his brother stood up for was right. “Standing up for justice has to be a part of our culture.”

morning.text:
Jantar Mantar July protests: Supreme Court asks enquiry panel to submit reports in a month on police crackdown, alleged brutality
The five-member committee told the court that its complaints portal became operational on October 14 but had received only a few complaints so far.
The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the high-powered enquiry committee (HPEC), examining complaints of police excesses and violence during the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)-led July protests at Jantar Mantar, to submit its fact-finding reports within a month, after the panel informed the court that its complaints portal became operational on October 14.
The five-member committee, formed in August under the chairmanship of former Supreme Court judge, justice (retd) R Subhash Reddy, informed the court in a confidential report that only a few complaints had been received on the portal, with no complainant appearing in person or approaching the committee through email.
The bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi said, “We would like the committee to start submitting its fact-finding reports.”
The court referred to its August 18 and September 10 orders, which had asked the committee to consider submitting reports on two priority issues: targeted violence, harassment and molestation of women protesters; and grievous harm and injuries allegedly caused to protesters by police and security personnel, including the need for interim compensation.
Posting the matter for December 2, the bench said, “The committee may submit an interim report on the priority issues identified by us.”
Also read: More complaints from cops than students over July 20 protest: SC-appointed panel
Complaints and Material for the Committee
The court asked the petitioners to encourage victims and complainants to file their representations with the committee. At the same time, it clarified that the panel need not wait indefinitely for complaints. “Whatever information and material is submitted by the parties, including material submitted by petitioners on behalf of the victims, will be examined and considered,” the bench said.
The court also said that since complainants were not required to disclose victims’ identities, petitioners could share with the HPEC material already submitted before the court, including copies of petitions and video clips attached to them.
The committee’s confidential report was circulated only among the judges. Senior advocate Monika Gusain, assisting the court as amicus curiae, said the reports were not being shared with her. Petitioners represented by senior advocates N Hariharan and Gopal Sankaranarayanan also said they were unable to assist the court without knowing the contents of the HPEC reports.
Also read: Supreme Court panel opens portal for complaints over violence on July 20 Delhi protest
The bench said the committee had not yet begun preparing action-taken reports on the 12 issues identified by the court in its August 18 order. “Unless we find something extraordinary requiring details of the complainants to be kept confidential, we would like to share the relevant contents of the reports,” it indicated.
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, opposed sharing the report with the petitioners. “The victims are not approaching the committee and instead, third parties are seeking to approach on their behalf. There may be the possibility of an exaggeration in the petition which is not there in reality. Someone may say there are 50 victims when there are only five,” he said.
Sankaranarayanan told the court that the HPEC appeared to be prioritising complaints filed directly by victims over material submitted by petitioners on their behalf. He cited a communication from the committee saying that the material submitted by the petitioner would be considered in “due course”.
The bench clarified that the committee was waiting for all material to be submitted before proceeding to examine it.
Also read: Pellet guns, harassment of women, cop injuries focus of SC panel's probe into CJP protest
Disciplinary Action Against Police
The bench also clarified that its August 18 order should not be interpreted as a direction to initiate disciplinary action against police personnel found to have committed excesses.
The August 18 order had said that the constitution of the HPEC would not prevent police authorities or security forces from taking administrative or disciplinary action against officers found to have violated conduct rules.
Citing this, petitioners claimed that no departmental action had been initiated against police personnel allegedly involved in the excesses.
“We would like to clarify two things: Our order is not a mandate. Second, we only clarified that the power of police authorities to discipline its employees is not cluttered by our order. If they decide to take action, it is under their purview,” the bench told the petitioners.
Mehta said police personnel had also suffered serious injuries and that the issue had been referred to the committee. “I will not put the cart before the horse. If the committee comes to the conclusion that there was any transgression on our part, we will obey it,” he said.
The bench said it would be in a better position to decide on each of the 12 issues once the committee submitted its reports. It also directed Delhi Police to file a comprehensive response to the petitions, while granting it liberty to submit separate affidavits on specific issues arising in the batch of petitions.
Also read: HPEC to prioritise complaints of sexual assault during NEET protests: SC
Petitions and Committee Membership
The petitions before the top court include those filed by members of Parliament, former civil servants, public-spirited individuals and lawyers, who accused police of using excessive force against students and other protesters at Jantar Mantar. The protesters had demanded the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The agitation was called off on July 25, following his resignation.
The court also entertained a petition filed by families of more than 200 police personnel who were injured while on duty during the protests.
Besides justice Reddy, the HPEC comprises former Punjab and Haryana high court chief justice Ravi Shankar Jha, former Delhi high court judge Shalinder Kaur, former CBI director Rishi Kumar Shukla and former Meghalaya director general of police LR Bishnoi.
On Thursday, the court received a letter from Bishnoi seeking permission to resign from the committee. It allowed his request and asked the panel to indicate whether it required a replacement.
